## About this case study

This case study replicates a published analysis. The paper's table and its
perfect-information results are reproduced exactly. Its value of *imperfect*
monitoring rests on a likelihood fitted to data that are not published, so that one
number is quoted, not recomputed, and the vignette instead works out what kind of
monitoring would be worth that much. The comparisons are in the test suite
(`test/fixtures/replications/luhede2024_weser.json`, `test/test_replications.jl`).

## The paper

Luhede, Yaqine, Bahmanbijari, Römer and Upmann (2024), "The value of information in
water quality monitoring and management", *Ecological Economics* 219:108128,
[doi:10.1016/j.ecolecon.2024.108128](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2024.108128),
CC BY 4.0. The input is Table 2 of the article.

**Decision.** Whether to take a management action against nutrient pollution on a
water body of the river Weser.

**Actions.** No action (`a0`, the `baseline`) or the action (`a1`), which is assumed
always to reach or keep the good state.

**States.** The water body is in a bad (`x0`) or a good (`x1`) ecological state under
the Water Framework Directive.

**Belief.** A prior probability of 0.1 that the state is good.

**Outcome.** Money: **the paper's valuation**, in millions of euros per year. A water
body in the good state is valued at 200 and the action costs 90, both taken by the
authors from the literature and from river-basin reports. Nothing here is valued by
this package.

```{julia}
using DecisionAnalysis
include(joinpath("..", "_common.jl"))
using Plots

actions = [:a0_no_action, :a1_action]
states = [:x0_bad, :x1_good]
# Table 2 of the paper: payoff v(a, x) in million EUR per year.
payoff = PayoffTable(actions, states, [0 200; 110 110])
problem = DecisionProblem(payoff, FiniteBelief(states, [9 // 10, 1 // 10]);
                          baseline=:a0_no_action)
md_table(["action", "expected payoff", "expected gain over no action", "chosen"],
         [[a, e, g, a in decide(problem, MaxExpectedUtility()).chosen]
          for (a, e, g) in zip(actions, aggregate(Expectation(), problem),
                               expected_gain_over_baseline(problem))])
```

## The published numbers

```{julia}
v0 = act_now_value(problem)
md_table(["quantity (million EUR per year)", "paper (Table 3)", "this package"],
         [["value under the prior", 110, v0],
          ["value with perfect information", 119, v0 + evpi(problem)],
          ["value of perfect information", 9, evpi(problem)]])
```

The paper then varies the prior probability `p` of the good state and the cost `c` of
the action. Its Figure 2 reports that at a medium cost of 100 the value of perfect
information peaks at `p = 0.5`, at 50 million euros per year, and that at a low cost
of 50 it peaks at `p = 0.75`.

```{julia}
general(p, c) = DecisionProblem(PayoffTable(actions, states, [0 200; 200-c 200-c]),
                                FiniteBelief(states, [1 - p, p]); baseline=:a0_no_action)
grid = (0:100) .// 100
plt = plot(; xlabel="prior probability of the good state", ylabel="EVPI (million EUR per year)",
           title="Value of perfect information by cost of the action (Figure 2)")
for c in (50, 100, 150)
    plot!(plt, Float64.(grid), [Float64(evpi(general(p, c))) for p in grid];
          label="cost $c")
end
png_figure(plt)
```

```{julia}
peak(c) = grid[argmax([evpi(general(p, c)) for p in grid])]
md_table(["cost of the action", "prior at which EVPI peaks", "EVPI there", "paper"],
         [[c, peak(c), evpi(general(peak(c), c)), note]
          for (c, note) in ((50, "peak at p = 0.75"), (100, "p = 0.5, up to 50"),
                            (150, "not stated"))])
```

The peak is where the two actions tie, `p = c / 200`: information is worth most to a
manager who is undecided.

## Imperfect monitoring

The paper's monitoring signal is a measurement of total nitrogen. Its likelihood is a
gamma distribution fitted to measurements from water bodies in the bad state and a
four-parameter beta distribution for those in the good state. With it the paper finds
a value of 112.21 with monitoring, so that monitoring is worth **2.21 million euros
per year** (95% interval 2.06 to 2.84), a quarter of the 9 million of perfect
information. The data are "available on request" and the fitted parameters are not
printed, so this number cannot be recomputed here. What can be done is to ask what a
monitoring programme must be like to be worth that.

### A single reading

Take the simplest programme: one reading that classifies the water body as good or
bad and is right with probability `q` in either state.

```{julia}
reading(q) = Experiment([q 1-q; 1-q q]; signals=[:reads_bad, :reads_good], states)
qs = (50:100) .// 100
plt = plot(Float64.(qs), [Float64(evsi(problem, reading(q))) for q in qs]; legend=false,
           xlabel="probability that a reading is right", ylabel="EVSI (million EUR per year)",
           title="Value of one reading")
hline!(plt, [2.21]; linestyle=:dash, color=:gray)
png_figure(plt)
```

```{julia}
useful = qs[findfirst(q -> information_can_change_decision(problem, reading(q)), qs)]
equivalent = qs[findfirst(q -> evsi(problem, reading(q)) >= 221 // 100, qs)]
md_table(["quantity", "accuracy of a reading"],
         [["first accuracy on the grid at which a reading can change the decision", useful],
          ["accuracy at which a reading is worth the paper's 2.21", equivalent]])
```

A reading that is right less than 11 times in 12 is worth nothing at all. The
prior is so firmly against the good state that a "good" reading from a poorer test
still leaves acting as the better choice, and information that cannot change the
action has no value (`information_can_change_decision` is equivalent to a positive
EVSI). The paper's 2.21 corresponds to a single reading that is right 94% of the time.

### Repeated readings

A programme usually takes several samples. With `n` independent readings, each right
with probability `q`, the signal is the number that read "good".

```{julia}
count_probability(n, k, q) = binomial(big(n), big(k)) * q^k * (1 - q)^(n - k)
function programme(n, q)
    q = Rational{BigInt}(q)
    L = [count_probability(n, k, s == 1 ? 1 - q : q) for k in 0:n, s in 1:2]   # s = 1: bad
    return Experiment(L; signals=[Symbol("good_", k) for k in 0:n], states)
end
ns = 1:25
plt = plot(; xlabel="number of readings", ylabel="EVSI (million EUR per year)",
           title="Value of a monitoring programme", legend=:bottomright)
for q in (7 // 10, 8 // 10, 9 // 10)
    plot!(plt, ns, [Float64(evsi(problem, programme(n, q))) for n in ns];
          label="each right with probability $(Float64(q))", marker=:circle, markersize=3)
end
hline!(plt, [9]; linestyle=:dash, color=:black, label="EVPI")
hline!(plt, [2.21]; linestyle=:dash, color=:gray, label="paper: 2.21")
png_figure(plt)
```

```{julia}
needed(q, target) = findfirst(n -> evsi(problem, programme(n, q)) >= target, 1:200)
md_table(["accuracy of each reading", "readings before the programme has any value",
          "readings to be worth 2.21", "readings to be worth 8 of the 9"],
         [[Float64(q), needed(q, 1 // 10^9), needed(q, 221 // 100), needed(q, 8)]
          for q in (7 // 10, 8 // 10, 9 // 10)])
```

The accuracies are ours, chosen to span poor to good tests; the paper's signal is
continuous and its likelihood unpublished.

### Net gain

The net gain of a programme is its EVSI less what it costs. The paper compares the two
in words but gives no monitoring cost, and none is assumed here. The EVSI is itself
the break-even: a programme is worth buying if and only if it costs less per year than
its EVSI. For a programme priced per reading, the table gives the largest price per
reading at which `n` readings still have a positive net gain, and the gain that the
last reading added.

```{julia}
q = 8 // 10
curve = [evsi(problem, programme(n, q)) for n in 0:25]
md_table(["readings", "EVSI", "break-even price per reading", "added by the last reading"],
         [[n, curve[n + 1], curve[n + 1] / n, curve[n + 1] - curve[n]]
          for n in (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 18, 25)]; digits=3)
```

The best number of readings depends on the price, so it is shown as a function of the
price and not at one assumed value:

```{julia}
prices = 0.01:0.01:1.0
best_n(k) = argmax([Float64(curve[n + 1]) - k * n for n in 0:25]) - 1
plt = plot(prices, best_n.(prices); legend=false, linetype=:steppost,
           xlabel="price per reading (million EUR per year)",
           ylabel="readings that maximise the net gain",
           title="Best programme against its price (accuracy 0.8)")
png_figure(plt)
```

```{julia}
free = optimal_design(problem, [Symbol("n_", n) => programme(n, q) for n in (5, 10, 15, 20)])
(criterion=free.criterion, best=free.best)
```

With no cost stated, `optimal_design` compares by EVSI alone and the largest programme
wins; it takes costs in the units of the payoff when there are some to give.

## What the package adds

### The value of monitoring when the prior is a range

The prior of 0.1 is an estimate. If all that can be said is that the probability of
the good state lies between 0.05 and 0.3, the value of a programme is a range too.

```{julia}
credal = DecisionProblem(payoff, CredalSet(states, [[19 // 20, 1 // 20], [7 // 10, 3 // 10]]);
                         baseline=:a0_no_action)
p10 = programme(10, 8 // 10)
r_perfect, r_sample = robust_evpi(credal), robust_evsi(credal, p10)
md_table(["quantity (million EUR per year)", "at prior 0.05", "at prior 0.3",
          "at the paper's prior, 0.1", "to a Γ-maximin manager"],
         [["value of perfect information", r_perfect.members..., evpi(problem), r_perfect.value],
          ["value of ten readings, each right with probability 0.8", r_sample.members...,
           evsi(problem, p10), r_sample.value]]; digits=2)
```

```{julia}
(lowest_evpi_over_the_set=r_perfect.lower, highest_evpi_over_the_set=r_perfect.upper)
```

The value of monitoring is several times larger at the optimistic end of the range
than at the prior the paper uses: there the manager is closer to undecided. Over the
set the EVPI runs from 4.5 to 27, both at its ends, because the prior at which the two
actions tie (0.55) lies outside it.

### Regret

```{julia}
regret_table(problem)
```

```{julia}
md_table(["rule", "choice"],
         [["expected payoff, prior 0.1", decide(problem, MaxExpectedUtility()).chosen],
          ["minimax regret", decide(problem, MinimaxRegret()).chosen],
          ["maximin", decide(problem, Maximin()).chosen]])
```

Acting is the choice under every rule: its worst regret is 90, the cost of an action
that turned out to be unnecessary, against 110 for failing to act on a water body in
the bad state.

## What to take away

- Table 3 of the paper is reproduced exactly: 110 under the prior, 119 with perfect
  information, an EVPI of 9 million euros per year in the paper's valuation; and so
  are the peaks of its Figure 2.
- The value of imperfect monitoring, 2.21, is not recomputed: the likelihood behind it
  is not published. It is what a single classification right 94% of the time would be
  worth.
- Below an accuracy of about 0.92 a single reading is worth nothing, because it cannot
  change the decision; several poorer readings can.
- The net gain needs a cost that the paper does not give. The EVSI is the break-even
  cost, and the best size of programme is given as a function of the price.
- Added here: the binomial monitoring programmes and their EVSI, the break-even
  prices, the value over a range of priors, and the regret table.
